Have agents verify callers by quizzing them on employment details held in the HR system
Require identity proofing comparable to initial enrollment before binding any replacement authenticator
Force an immediate password reset across all executive accounts after the incident
explanations: This confuses authenticator strength with recovery-channel strength: the attack never touched the authenticator itself, and even hardware keys can be replaced through the same weak help desk re-enrollment path.
Employment details are knowledge-based verification; they are discoverable through research, social media, and prior breaches, so a well-prepared social engineer can still pass the quiz.

The exploited weakness is that binding a new authenticator, which is equivalent to reissuing the credential, was allowed on the strength of a phone call. Requiring re-verification at a rigor matching original proofing closes that recovery loophole.
Passwords were never compromised in this attack, so resetting them is incident theater; the account-recovery process, not the knowledge factor, is the broken control.

stem: System administrators at a firm each use a single account holding domain administrator rights for all activity, including email, web browsing, and routine office tasks. Which practice should the security manager mandate?
options: Move the administrators onto one shared admin account protected by a much stronger password
Issue each administrator separate standard and privileged accounts, using the privileged one only for admin tasks
Require multifactor authentication whenever the administrators read their corporate email
Limit each administrator to local administrator rights on their own assigned workstation
explanations: A shared account destroys individual accountability and widens credential exposure; the problem here is privilege mixed into risky daily activity, not password strength.

Separating everyday identity from privileged identity means phishing, drive-by downloads, and mail-borne malware land on an account with ordinary rights, sharply reducing the blast radius of the most common compromises.
MFA on email is a useful control but misreads the exposure: the danger is that browsing and email happen inside a domain-admin security context, which MFA on the mailbox does not change.

This confuses endpoint-local privilege with domain privilege; the administrators legitimately need domain rights for their duties, so the fix is separating when those rights are in play, not removing them.

stem: A university federates with a cloud research service via SAML. The service only needs to know a user is current faculty, but the identity provider's default configuration releases full name, national ID number, and department to every relying party. What should the identity architect do?
options: Encrypt the SAML assertions so the attributes cannot be read while they are in transit
Have the service sign a data processing agreement covering the released attributes
Replace SAML with OpenID Connect, since it shares fewer user attributes by default
Configure per-relying-party attribute release limited to an affiliation or entitlement claim
explanations: Assertion encryption protects confidentiality against interceptors, but the relying party still decrypts and receives everything; transit protection is not data minimization.
A contract is an administrative safeguard for data already shared; it neither prevents overexposure nor helps if the service is breached, whereas not sending the data removes the exposure.
This is a protocol myth: both SAML and OIDC release whatever attributes or claims the IdP is configured to send, so swapping protocols does not by itself minimize anything.

Federation should release only the attributes each relying party genuinely needs; asserting affiliation without identifiers applies least privilege to identity data and eliminates unnecessary disclosure of the national ID.

stem: A banking consortium wants customers to prove employment or account standing to third parties without the verifier contacting the issuing bank each time, and with the customer choosing which claims to disclose in each interaction. Which identity model BEST fits these goals?
options: Decentralized identity with cryptographically verifiable credentials held in a user-controlled wallet
A central OAuth authorization server that issues scoped access tokens to each verifier
SAML federation in which each third-party verifier becomes a relying party of the bank's IdP
An enterprise directory whose records are synchronized out to each verifier using SCIM
explanations: Verifiable credentials are signed once by the issuer, stored by the holder, and checked cryptographically by any verifier without issuer involvement, and wallets support disclosing selected claims, matching both stated goals.
OAuth is delegated authorization: the authorization server must participate in each grant, and tokens convey permission to call APIs rather than portable, selectively disclosable identity claims.

SAML federation requires the bank's IdP to be online and involved in every authentication event, and its assertions carry the attribute set the IdP chooses, not claims the customer selects per interaction.
SCIM is an account provisioning protocol; replicating directory records to every verifier is the opposite of minimal, user-controlled disclosure and creates copies the customer cannot govern.

stem: A SaaS provider supports both SP-initiated and IdP-initiated SAML single sign-on. Its security architect observes that one flow forces the service to accept assertions it never asked for. Which statement BEST captures the risk-based guidance?
options: IdP-initiated SSO is safer because the IdP always authenticates the user before any assertion is ever sent to the service
Prefer SP-initiated SSO, because unsolicited IdP-initiated assertions cannot be matched to a request the SP generated, easing injection and replay
The two flows carry identical risk because the assertions are digitally signed by the IdP in either flow
IdP-initiated SSO should be preferred because it eliminates the redirect step that an attacker could otherwise tamper with
explanations: This confuses where authentication happens with how the response is bound: the IdP authenticates the user in both flows, so authentication order is not what differentiates their risk.

In SP-initiated SSO the service issues a request ID and can verify the response answers it, giving replay and injection protection; unsolicited IdP-initiated responses lack that request binding, so the SP must accept assertions with weaker context.

Signatures prove the issuer and integrity of an assertion, but they cannot prove the SP asked for it; a validly signed assertion can still be injected into a victim's browser session in the unsolicited flow.

This inverts the redirect's role: the SP-initiated redirect carries the authentication request whose ID later binds the response (via InResponseTo) to a real login attempt, so removing it removes a safeguard rather than an attack surface.

stem: HR clerks need to look up employee office locations and reporting managers but must never see salary or health fields stored in the same employee records. Which authorization approach MOST directly enforces this requirement?
options: Context-dependent access control evaluating the time, location, and device of each query
Role-based access control granting the clerks an HR role with rights on the employee table
Content-dependent access control that exposes only permitted fields, such as restricted database views
Field-level encryption applied to the salary and health columns in the database
explanations: Context-dependent control decides based on the circumstances of access, not on what the data contains; a clerk querying at a valid time and place would still see every column.
A role granted at table level is too coarse: RBAC answers who may touch the object, but the requirement is to restrict which parts of each record are visible, which the role alone cannot express.

Restricting access based on the data itself, classically implemented as views that project only approved columns, is content-dependent access control and enforces the field-level restriction precisely.

Encryption is a cryptographic confidentiality control, not a per-user authorization decision; if the application holds the key, clerks see decrypted values, and if not, even authorized payroll users are blocked.

stem: Warehouse workers use handheld scanner applications that display only the three menu functions their job requires; all other functions are hidden or greyed out and are also rejected by the server. Which access control concept does this illustrate?
options: A constrained user interface that restricts the functions available to the user
Attribute-based access control evaluating user and environmental attributes per request
A capability list enumerating the objects and rights held by each warehouse worker
Security through obscurity, because the unavailable functions are merely being hidden
explanations: Limiting what a user can even see or invoke through menus, greyed-out options, or restricted shells is the textbook constrained user interface, here properly backed by server-side enforcement.
ABAC is a policy-evaluation model that computes decisions from attributes at request time; nothing in the scenario describes attribute-driven policy, only a deliberately limited interface.
A capability list is a data structure binding a subject to object rights; it describes how rights are recorded, not the presentation-layer technique of removing functions from view.
Obscurity would mean hiding is the only protection; because the server also rejects unauthorized functions, the hidden menus are a legitimate enforcement-backed interface restriction.

stem: An audit at a bank finds users gaining access to sensitive shares through chains of five or more nested directory groups, and no administrator can state what a given user can effectively reach. Which remediation BEST restores manageable authorization?
options: Assign permissions directly to individual user accounts to eliminate all group ambiguity
Increase how often managers recertify each user's directly assigned group memberships
Migrate the sensitive file shares to mandatory access control with classification labels
Impose group governance limiting nesting depth, assigning an owner per group, and reviewing effective access
explanations: Direct assignments feel precise but abandon scalable administration: thousands of per-user entries quickly drift, resist review, and recreate the opacity in a worse form.
This audits the wrong layer: the risky access arrives transitively through nesting, so recertifying only direct memberships, however frequently, never surfaces what users actually reach.

MAC solves a different problem, enforcing classification dominance in high-assurance environments; imposing labels on a commercial bank's shares is disproportionate and does not untangle group sprawl.

The failure is ungoverned group structure, so the fix is structural: bounded nesting, accountable owners, and reviews computed on resultant effective permissions restore the ability to know and manage who can access what.

stem: Regional IT help desks need only to reset passwords and unlock accounts for users in their own region, yet today every help desk technician holds full domain administrator rights. What is the BEST correction?
options: Enroll the technicians in a PAM vault that records every domain administrator session they open
Create delegated administration roles scoped to reset and unlock rights over each region's user accounts
Require dual authorization from a second technician before any password reset is performed
Rotate the domain administrator credentials automatically at the end of every help desk shift
explanations: Session recording is monitoring, not least privilege: the technicians would retain domain-wide power, and the organization would merely have better footage of any misuse or compromise.

Delegation grants exactly the two operations required, bounded to each region's organizational scope, eliminating standing domain-admin exposure while fully supporting the help desk mission; this is least privilege applied to administration.
Dual control adds friction to a routine, high-volume task and addresses collusion risk, but each technician still holds vastly excessive standing authority the task does not need.
Credential rotation shortens how long a stolen password works but does nothing about authorization scope; while on shift, every technician still wields rights over the entire domain.

stem: An internal workflow tool integrates with the corporate email platform through OAuth. Developers registered it to request the full-mailbox-access scope even though the tool only sends notification messages. What should the security reviewer require?
options: Switch the integration to the client credentials grant so no user consent screens appear
Store the integration's refresh token inside the enterprise secrets management vault
Re-register the application for the narrowest scope that permits sending mail only
Shorten the access token lifetime so the broad scope expires much more quickly
explanations: Changing the grant type changes how tokens are obtained, not what they authorize; a client-credentials token with the same broad scope carries the identical excessive privilege.
Vaulting protects the token from theft but does not reduce what a stolen or misused token can do; a well-guarded key to the whole mailbox is still a key to the whole mailbox.

Scopes are the least-privilege mechanism of delegated authorization: requesting only send-mail rights means any compromise of the tool or its tokens exposes one narrow capability instead of every user's full mailbox content.
Lifetime bounds the replay window, not the breadth of authority, and the refresh token continually renews the same over-broad access, so the excessive privilege effectively persists.

stem: A payroll specialist who left the company two years ago is rehired into a marketing role. The IT team proposes reactivating her archived account to save setup time. What should the identity management lead direct?
options: Provision a fresh set of entitlements through the standard joiner process for the new role
Reactivate the account but require a password reset and new MFA enrollment before first login
Reactivate the account and flag it for scrutiny during the next quarterly recertification
Provision a new account while leaving the old one active to preserve access to historical data
explanations: A rehire is a new joiner for authorization purposes: building access from the current role's requirements prevents the old payroll entitlements from silently returning with the identity.
This confuses refreshing authenticators with reviewing authorization; new credentials on the old account still resurrect every stale payroll entitlement attached to it.
Reactivate-then-review leaves a marketing employee holding payroll access for up to a quarter, choosing a delayed detective check where a preventive control was available on day one.
Historical data belongs under records retention, not a live login; keeping the old account active creates a second, unmonitored identity with obsolete privileges attached.

stem: New hires automatically receive access to over forty applications on day one because the onboarding template has grown for years as departments added useful systems. Recertification campaigns keep flagging large volumes of unused entitlements. What is the BEST structural fix?
options: Deploy automation that revokes any entitlement that has gone unused for ninety consecutive days
Shorten the recertification campaign cycle for these entitlements from annual to quarterly
Require each new hire's manager to review and approve the full onboarding template individually
Cut birthright access to a minimal common baseline and grant the remainder through role-based or approved requests
explanations: Usage-based revocation treats the symptom downstream: the template keeps regranting excess at every hire, and automated removal risks breaking legitimate but infrequently exercised access.
More frequent reviews of a structurally bloated baseline multiply reviewer workload and invite rubber-stamping; the campaign frequency was never the reason the excess exists.
Asking a manager to approve a forty-application bundle produces one habitual signature, not forty considered decisions; bulk approval is where rubber-stamping begins.

The root cause is an inflated birthright baseline, so shrinking day-one access to what everyone truly needs and routing the rest through roles or request-and-approval stops over-provisioning at its source.

stem: During access recertification for a finance data warehouse, line managers approve their staff's access but admit they do not know what the data contains or who should legitimately use it. Who is BEST positioned to certify access to this data set?
options: The database administrator, who understands the schema, grants, and permission structures
The finance data owner, who is accountable for the data and its authorized business uses
The chief information security officer, as the senior executive accountable for security
Each user's line manager, because they know their own employees' current job duties
explanations: The DBA is the custodian: skilled at implementing and maintaining access, but custodians act on the owner's decisions and should not be the authority deciding who ought to have access.

Owners carry business accountability for their data set and know its sensitivity and legitimate use cases, so certification decisions about who should access it belong with them, informed by managers on personnel context.

The CISO governs the recertification program and its standards but cannot meaningfully judge access needs for every business data set; pushing per-dataset decisions to the CISO recreates uninformed sign-off at a higher pay grade.
Managers know their people but, as the scenario itself shows, not the data; certification by someone ignorant of what is being accessed is exactly the rubber-stamp pattern the process must escape.

stem: A cloud security review finds thousands of service accounts, API keys, and workload identities; many have no identifiable owner, and several belonged to projects cancelled years ago. Which action should the IAM program take FIRST?
options: Rotate every discovered credential immediately to invalidate any copies already stolen
Migrate all of the service accounts into the enterprise secrets vault for central control
Build an inventory of the non-human identities with assigned owners and lifecycle status before remediating
Delete every account that shows no authentication activity within the past twelve months
explanations: Mass rotation without knowing what each credential feeds will break unknown production dependencies, and it hardens identities that should not exist at all rather than establishing control.
Vault onboarding presumes you know each account's purpose, owner, and consumers; vaulting an unmanaged sprawl merely relocates the mystery into better-protected storage.

Non-human identities can only be governed once they are known: an inventory with accountable owners and lifecycle state tells the program what to retire, rotate, or vault, making every subsequent remediation safe and prioritized.
Dormancy is weak evidence for machine identities, where disaster recovery paths and annual batch jobs may authenticate rarely; deletion without owner and impact analysis risks self-inflicted outages.

stem: Departing employees keep appearing as active users in several SaaS tools that business units purchased directly on corporate cards; none of the tools are connected to the corporate IdP or provisioning system. Which response BEST addresses the root cause?
options: Mandate SSO and provisioning integration as a purchase condition for SaaS, with ongoing discovery of unsanctioned apps
Add the SaaS tools identified so far to the manual offboarding checklist used by the service desk
Prohibit business units from purchasing any software outside the central IT procurement process
Extend the quarterly user access review campaigns to cover each of the discovered SaaS applications
explanations: Leavers persist because these apps sit outside the identity lifecycle; conditioning purchases on IdP and provisioning integration brings every future app into automated deprovisioning, and discovery finds the ones that slip through.
A manual checklist covers only today's known tools, depends on human diligence, and does nothing about the next uncontrolled purchase; it patches instances while leaving the pattern intact.

Pure prohibition tends to push the same purchases onto personal cards and free tiers, worsening visibility; governing the channel with security conditions manages the risk without driving it underground.
Reviews are detective and quarterly, so a leaver could retain access for months, and like the checklist they reach only the applications the organization already happens to know about.

stem: A native mobile app receives OAuth authorization codes through a custom URL scheme. Security testing shows that a malicious app on the same device could register the identical scheme and intercept the returned code. Which control MOST directly mitigates this interception?
options: Use the implicit grant so that no authorization code is ever exposed on the device
Embed a confidential client secret in the mobile app to authenticate its token requests
Prompt the user to re-enter their credentials at the moment the code is redeemed for tokens
Implement PKCE so redeeming the code requires the code verifier that only the initiating app holds
explanations: The implicit grant returns tokens directly in the redirect, exposing the more valuable artifact through the same interceptable channel; it is deprecated for precisely this class of weakness.
A mobile binary is a public client: any secret compiled into it can be extracted from the package, so the malicious app could present the same secret alongside the stolen code.
Code redemption is a back-channel call from app to token endpoint with no user interaction; a user prompt cannot bind the code to the legitimate application making that call.

PKCE binds the code to the app instance that started the flow: the token endpoint only honors redemption accompanied by the original code verifier, so an intercepted code is worthless to the malicious app.

stem: During a purple-team exercise, testers compromise a legacy application server configured for unconstrained Kerberos delegation and harvest forwarded TGTs for every user who connected, including domain administrators. Which remediation BEST reduces this exposure?
options: Enforce substantially shorter Kerberos ticket lifetimes across the entire domain
Replace unconstrained delegation with constrained or resource-based delegation limited to the required services
Move the legacy application server into a separately administered Kerberos realm
Mandate smart card logon for every account that holds domain administrator rights
explanations: Lifetime tuning shrinks how long a stolen ticket works but does not stop the server from receiving and exposing users' TGTs; fresh tickets are harvested with every new connection.

Unconstrained delegation hands the server a copy of each connecting user's TGT, an impersonate-anyone-anywhere credential; constrained forms let the server act only toward enumerated services and stop the wholesale TGT exposure.
Realm separation redraws administrative boundaries, but with trust in place credentials still flow to the delegating server; the dangerous delegation configuration survives the move intact.

Smart cards strengthen how the TGT is initially obtained, yet the resulting TGT is forwarded to the server all the same; protecting privileged accounts requires barring them from delegation, not just hardening their logon.

stem: A penetration tester obtains a valid ID token issued by the corporate OpenID Connect provider to a low-security internal app, then presents it to the HR portal, which accepts it and establishes a session. The token's signature verifies correctly. What is the underlying flaw?
options: The identity provider's private signing key must have been compromised by the tester
The HR portal should have demanded an OAuth access token rather than an ID token
The HR portal fails to validate the audience claim, so tokens minted for other clients are accepted
The token lifetime is configured too long, allowing it to be replayed to a second application
explanations: No key compromise is needed: the token is genuine and correctly signed; the attack works because a legitimate token for one application is honored by another, which is a validation failure at the relying party.

Token-type pedantry misses the flaw: an access token presented cross-service is abusable in exactly the same way unless its intended audience or resource is checked, so swapping types alone changes nothing.

Every OIDC relying party must verify the token was issued for its own client identifier; skipping the audience check turns any token from the shared provider into a skeleton key across all relying applications.
A freshly issued token can be replayed to the wrong application within seconds, so expiry settings are irrelevant; lifetime bounds how long the mistake works, not whether it works.

stem: A company enforces MFA on its cloud email portal, yet an attacker using password spraying gains mailbox access with passwords alone. Logs show the successful logins arrived through an IMAP basic-authentication endpoint. What should the security team do FIRST?
options: Disable legacy authentication protocols that cannot enforce the MFA policy, after identifying dependent clients
Strengthen the password composition and complexity requirements to defeat spraying attempts
Deploy stronger multifactor methods, such as hardware security keys, for all mailbox users
Block sign-in attempts originating from countries where the company has no business presence
explanations: The MFA policy is being bypassed, not beaten: basic-auth protocols never present a second-factor challenge, so closing that path, with a dependency check to avoid breaking legacy mail clients, removes the attack channel itself.
Spraying tries common passwords that already satisfy most composition rules, and some accounts will always hold weak-but-compliant secrets; hardening the first factor leaves the MFA bypass wide open.
This upgrades a control the attacker never encounters; whether the second factor is an app prompt or a hardware key is irrelevant on an endpoint that skips the second factor entirely.
Geo-blocking is a network heuristic trivially evaded with proxies and cloud hosts in permitted regions; it narrows the attacker's source options without closing the authentication gap.

stem: A security manager installs cameras covering the entrances to a records storage room. The cameras record continuously, and footage is reviewed only after an incident is reported; nobody monitors the feeds in real time. Which control category BEST describes this CCTV deployment?
options: Preventive control
Deterrent control
Detective control
Corrective control
explanations: Preventive controls physically stop an act before it occurs, like a locked door or a turnstile; a camera that merely records cannot block anyone from entering, so equating visibility with prevention is a category error.

Visible cameras do carry deterrent value by discouraging would-be intruders, but the deployment's stated function - reviewing footage only after an incident - is discovering and reconstructing events, which is detection, not deterrence.

Because the footage is examined only after something has happened, the cameras serve to identify, verify, and reconstruct incidents after the fact - the defining characteristic of a detective control.
Corrective controls fix damage or restore operations after an incident, such as restoring from backup; recording and reviewing evidence does not remediate anything.

stem: During security awareness training, a new analyst asks why typing a username at a login prompt is not enough to be granted access, since the system then 'knows who they are.' Which concept explains what supplying a username actually accomplishes?
options: Identification - the user asserts an identity that has not yet been proven
Authentication - the system has verified that the user is who they claim to be
Authorization - the system has determined what resources the user may access
Accountability - the system can now reliably attribute actions to the user
explanations: A username is only an unverified claim of identity; the system must still validate that claim with a credential such as a password, token, or biometric before placing any trust in it.
Authentication is the act of proving the claimed identity with a credential; merely stating a username proves nothing, which is exactly the analyst's confusion between claiming and proving.
Authorization decides what an already-authenticated subject may do; it cannot meaningfully occur before the identity claim has been verified.
Accountability depends on actions being logged against authenticated, unique identities; an unproven assertion of a username cannot reliably attribute anything to anyone.

stem: A facilities team connects a new building-automation controller to the corporate network. The installation guide, freely downloadable from the vendor's website, lists the administrator username and password that every unit ships with. What should the security team require FIRST before the device goes live?
options: Place the controller on an isolated VLAN behind a dedicated firewall
Change the default administrative credentials to unique, strong replacements
Enable detailed logging of all administrative access to the device
Verify that the controller is running the latest vendor firmware version
explanations: Network isolation is a valuable compensating layer, but it leaves a publicly documented credential valid - anyone who finds any path to the device can still log straight in; segmentation is not a substitute for credential hygiene.

The default credentials are published for the whole world to read, so the device is effectively protected by no secret at all; replacing them removes the most immediate and trivially exploitable access path before exposure begins.
Logging is a detective measure; it would record misuse of the well-known default password rather than prevent it.
Current firmware fixes software vulnerabilities, but a documented default password works perfectly on a fully patched device - patching addresses a different weakness.

stem: An employee is approved for a six-month unpaid sabbatical and is expected to return to the same role. What is the BEST way to handle the employee's user account during the absence?
options: Delete the account and provision a brand-new identity when the employee returns
Leave the account active but force a password change before the employee departs
Transfer the account credentials to the employee's manager to cover urgent tasks
Disable the account, retain its data and entitlements, and re-enable it upon verified return
explanations: Deletion is the end-of-lifecycle step for terminations; applying it to a planned leave destroys mailbox and data linkages and forces needless re-provisioning - it confuses a leaver with someone on leave.
An active but unused account is a standing target for months with nobody present to notice misuse; a fresh password does not remove that exposure.
Handing credentials to anyone else destroys individual accountability; coverage needs should be met by delegating rights to the manager's own identity, never by credential sharing.
Suspending the account removes the attack surface of an unattended active login while preserving the identity, data, and entitlements for a clean, verified reactivation when the employee returns.

stem: A phishing investigation reveals that many employees reuse a single memorized password across dozens of external business websites that cannot be integrated with the company's SSO. Which measure would BEST reduce this credential-reuse risk?
options: Enforce stricter password complexity rules on all corporate systems
Require employees to change their passwords every 60 days
Deploy an enterprise password manager that generates and stores unique credentials per site
Block employee access to external websites that are not integrated with corporate SSO
explanations: Complexity rules shape what a single password looks like but do nothing to stop that same strong password from being reused everywhere - strength and uniqueness are different properties.
Routine rotation typically produces predictable variants of the same password and does not break reuse across sites; current guidance discourages scheduled expiration for exactly this reason.
A password manager removes the human-memory bottleneck that drives reuse, letting every site have a distinct random credential so a breach of one external site no longer unlocks the rest.
Blocking every non-SSO site would halt legitimate business activity; it treats an authentication-hygiene weakness as a web-filtering problem.

stem: During design review of a new data center, the security architect wants all electronic door locks to remain locked whenever power is lost, but the fire marshal objects with respect to the emergency exit doors. How should this conflict be resolved?
options: Configure egress doors to fail-safe (unlock) on power loss and add compensating controls such as alarms, guards, and cameras
Keep all doors fail-secure because protecting the assets inside is the facility's primary mission
Install uninterruptible power for the locks so a power loss never actually occurs
Compromise by configuring half of the egress doors fail-secure and the other half fail-safe
explanations: Life safety always takes precedence over asset protection: occupants must be able to exit during an emergency, and the security gap created by unlocked egress doors is then covered with compensating detective and deterrent measures.
This inverts the fundamental priority order - human life outranks any asset, and safety codes prohibit configurations that could trap occupants to protect property.

Battery backup only postpones the condition; batteries deplete and fires can sever circuits, so engineering around the requirement does not satisfy the principle that people must always be able to egress.
Emergency egress requirements apply to every designated exit path; leaving some exits locked during an evacuation recreates the exact trapped-occupant hazard the fire marshal is preventing.

stem: Employees connect through a VPN, and once connected they can reach nearly every internal application. After a stolen laptop with cached VPN credentials was used to roam the network, the CISO wants a strategy that no longer grants broad access simply for being 'inside.' Which approach BEST meets this goal?
options: Add a second authentication factor to the VPN login process
Adopt a zero trust model that authorizes each application request based on user identity, device posture, and context
Perform a network access control health check on every endpoint before admitting it to the network
Divide the internal network into multiple VLANs separated by internal firewalls
explanations: MFA hardens the front door but preserves the flawed model: after one successful login, the session still inherits broad network-wide reach - authentication strength is being confused with the authorization model.

Zero trust removes the assumption that network location implies trustworthiness; every request to every application is evaluated against identity, device health, and context, so a compromised endpoint or credential no longer roams freely.
NAC admission checks are point-in-time gate decisions; once an endpoint is admitted it again enjoys location-based trust for everything behind the gate.
Segmentation shrinks the blast radius but access within each zone is still granted by network position rather than per-request evaluation of the requester.

stem: A software vendor must connect remotely each month to maintain a hospital's critical clinical system. The contract requires the hospital to be able to demonstrate exactly what the vendor's engineers did during each maintenance window. Which control BEST satisfies this requirement?
options: Have the vendor sign a nondisclosure and acceptable-use agreement before each maintenance window
Require the vendor's engineers to authenticate with multifactor authentication
Review the clinical system's native event logs after each maintenance window
Route vendor connections through a privileged access gateway that records the full interactive session
explanations: Agreements set obligations and consequences, but they are administrative instruments - they cannot show after the fact which commands were actually executed on the system.
MFA raises confidence in who connected; it says nothing about what that person did once connected, which is what the contract demands.
Native event logs are frequently incomplete for interactive and GUI work, and a privileged session can alter them; they rarely reconstruct the full activity independently.
A privileged access gateway that captures keystrokes and screen video creates an independent, tamper-resistant record of the entire session, directly proving what was done during each window.

stem: A company is selecting a biometric system for its main employee entrance, where about 4,000 people arrive during a 45-minute morning peak. Two shortlisted products have nearly identical crossover error rates and similar pricing. Which factor should MOST influence the final selection?
options: The false acceptance rate each product achieves at its default threshold setting
Verification speed and how willingly employees will accept using the modality
The storage size of each product's biometric template in the database
The physiological uniqueness of the trait each modality measures
explanations: Accuracy is already established as equivalent through the comparable crossover error rates, and thresholds can be tuned on either product - re-litigating FAR ignores what the CER comparison has settled.

At a high-volume entrance, throughput and user acceptance decide whether the system works operationally: a slow or intrusive modality creates queues, frustration, and bypass workarounds that damage security more than any marginal accuracy difference.
Templates are measured in kilobytes; storage is a trivial cost consideration next to daily operational fit for thousands of users.
The uniqueness of the underlying trait is an input to accuracy and is already reflected in the measured error rates the stem holds equal.

stem: During a red-team exercise, testers unlocked several employees' tablets by holding printed photographs of the device owners in front of the facial recognition camera. What is the BEST remediation?
options: Require facial recognition that performs presentation attack (liveness) detection such as depth and motion analysis
Raise the matching threshold so the algorithm demands a much closer facial match
Re-enroll all employees to capture higher-resolution reference templates
Increase the lockout penalty after failed facial recognition attempts
explanations: The attack presented an artifact of the genuine enrolled user, so matching succeeded legitimately; liveness detection verifies that a live human - not a photo, mask, or screen - is in front of the sensor, which is precisely the gap exploited.
A stricter threshold rejects poor matches, but a good photograph of the enrolled user is a good match and will still pass - this confuses matching accuracy with spoof detection.
Sharper reference templates improve matching quality in both directions and may make a quality photograph match even more reliably.
Lockouts throttle guessing attacks; a photo spoof of the right person typically succeeds on the first attempt, so the counter never engages.

stem: To cut help-desk calls, an IT director proposes password synchronization so each user's single password is replicated to the mainframe, the ERP system, and several legacy applications with widely varying security postures. What is the MOST significant risk of this approach?
options: Users will still have to log in to each application separately, so convenience will not improve much
The synchronized environment becomes single sign-on and inherits SSO session hijacking risks
A compromise of the weakest participating system exposes a password that is valid on every system
Replication delays after each password change will repeatedly lock users out of some applications
explanations: Separate logins do persist under synchronization, but that is a convenience limitation, not the significant security risk the question asks about.

Synchronization copies a credential between password stores; it creates no shared session or token, so SSO-specific session hijacking does not apply - this confuses password sync with true single sign-on.

The shared secret is now only as safe as the weakest system that stores it: cracking a legacy application's poorly hashed password file yields a credential that also opens the mainframe and the ERP system.
Propagation lag is a real operational nuisance, but it is transient and self-correcting - far less severe than cross-system credential exposure.

stem: A retailer plans to let employees of a new logistics partner access its shipment portal through federated login using the partner's identity provider. Before any technical integration work begins, what should the retailer do FIRST?
options: Exchange SAML metadata and token-signing certificates with the partner's engineers
Conduct a penetration test of the partner's identity provider infrastructure
Require the partner to enforce multifactor authentication for all portal users
Negotiate a federation agreement defining required assurance levels, liabilities, and attribute handling
explanations: Metadata and certificate exchange is the technical onboarding step; doing it first builds a live trust relationship before any rules governing that trust exist.

Assessment of the partner may form part of due diligence, but what must be tested and to what standard flows from the agreement - and testing another organization's systems requires that contractual authorization anyway.
An MFA mandate is one specific requirement that belongs inside the negotiated assurance terms; imposing it piecemeal is not a substitute for defining the trust framework.

In federation the retailer will grant access based on assertions it did not create, so the parties must first codify authentication strength, liability for false assertions, provisioning duties, and privacy handling - the governance foundation that all technical work then implements.

stem: Enterprise single sign-on failed for four hours when the token-signing certificate on the identity provider expired unnoticed. Which measure BEST prevents a recurrence?
options: Implement certificate lifecycle management with expiry monitoring and staged key rollover published in federation metadata
Issue the replacement signing certificate with a much longer validity period
Configure relying applications to accept assertions signed with an expired certificate during a grace period
Switch the identity provider to a self-signed signing certificate that the organization fully controls
explanations: Tracking expiry dates, alerting well in advance, and publishing the successor key in federation metadata so relying parties trust both keys during cutover eliminates both the surprise and the outage window.
A longer validity period merely postpones the same unmanaged cliff while widening the exposure window if the signing key is ever compromised - frequency reduction is not lifecycle management.
Accepting expired signatures deliberately weakens assertion validation, the very control that blocks forged logins; trading integrity for availability is the wrong resolution.
Self-signed certificates expire too; who issued the certificate is unrelated to whether anyone is tracking and rolling it over.

stem: A finance department depends on a 20-year-old application that supports only its own built-in username and password form and cannot be modified. The IAM program requires every application to sit behind enterprise SSO with MFA. What is the BEST way to bring this application into compliance?
options: Rewrite the application to natively support OpenID Connect before the program deadline
Front the application with an SSO gateway that enforces modern authentication and then injects vaulted credentials into the legacy login form
Synchronize the application's local passwords with the enterprise directory
Exempt the application and compensate with a stronger password policy for its local accounts
explanations: Modernization is the ideal end state, but the stem says the application cannot be modified; a rewrite is a long-term project, not an achievable control for the current requirement - the strategic ideal is being confused with a feasible measure.

A reverse-proxy or enterprise SSO gateway lets users authenticate once with enterprise MFA while the gateway replays stored credentials to the unchanged legacy form, delivering SSO and MFA enforcement without touching the application.
Password synchronization aligns secrets across stores but provides neither single sign-on nor a second factor; users still authenticate directly to the weak legacy form.
An exemption formally accepts the exposure the program was created to remove, and no password policy can add a second authentication factor.

stem: An identity governance rollout stalls because the provisioning engine receives conflicting values for employees' departments, managers, and job codes from the HR system, the ERP directory, and a legacy phone directory. What should the IAM team do to resolve this?
options: Configure the engine to accept whichever source updated each attribute most recently
Let employees review and correct their own profile attributes through a self-service portal
Designate an authoritative source for each attribute and synchronize all other systems from it
Have the help desk manually reconcile conflicting records as provisioning errors are reported
explanations: A last-writer-wins rule makes entitlements depend on update timing rather than truth: a stale system syncing late silently overwrites correct data - recency is being mistaken for authority.
Self-asserted attributes cannot drive access decisions; employees could alter the very values, such as department and manager, that determine their entitlements and approval routing.

Provisioning logic is only as reliable as its inputs; declaring one system of record per attribute - typically HR for organizational data - gives every downstream access decision a single, defensible source of truth.
Manual reconciliation treats symptoms one ticket at a time and can never keep pace with continuous joiner, mover, and leaver churn.

stem: An internal audit finds that many entitlements in the ERP system were granted directly by IT administrators after informal chat messages, with no record of who authorized the access. Which change BEST addresses the audit finding?
options: Require administrators to record the requester's name in the ticket queue after granting access
Run a one-time cleanup removing entitlements that nobody can currently explain
Restrict ERP entitlement changes to a smaller group of the most senior administrators
Route all access requests through a workflow requiring documented approval from the resource owner before provisioning occurs
explanations: Recording who asked still leaves the administrator acting as both approver and implementer; the missing element is documented authorization by someone accountable for the resource, not better note-taking.
A cleanup addresses today's unexplained entitlements, but the next informal chat request recreates the problem because the process defect remains untouched.
Concentrating the capability in fewer hands shrinks who can make undocumented grants, yet any of those administrators can still provision access with no approval evidence.
A request-approve-provision workflow separates asking, authorizing, and implementing, and generates the audit trail proving every entitlement was approved by the accountable owner before it existed.

stem: A penetration test showed that SQL injection in a customer portal yielded complete control of the database because the web application connects using an account holding database administrator rights. Beyond fixing the injection flaw itself, which access control change is MOST important?
options: Reconnect the application through a dedicated account limited to the specific tables and procedures it needs
Store the application's database password in a secrets vault with automatic rotation
Deploy a web application firewall in front of the customer portal
Encrypt the customer database using transparent data encryption
explanations: Whatever the application is authorized to do, an attacker exploiting it can do; enforcing least privilege on the service account caps the blast radius of any future application-layer compromise to the data the portal genuinely needs.

Vaulting and rotation protect the credential from theft, but an exploited application uses the live credential legitimately - rotating a secret does not reduce what the authenticated session is authorized to do.
A WAF is a compensating filter that novel payloads can evade; it leaves the excessive authorization behind it completely intact.
Transparent data encryption defends data at rest against media theft; an authorized connected session reads decrypted data regardless of it.

stem: A DevOps team's build pipeline authenticates to the cloud provider using API keys created three years ago and stored in the pipeline's configuration. A cloud security review flags the keys as a critical finding. Which remediation BEST eliminates this class of risk?
options: Move the API keys into a secrets manager and rotate them automatically every 24 hours
Establish workload identity federation so pipeline jobs exchange signed platform identity tokens for short-lived cloud credentials
Encrypt the pipeline configuration files that currently contain the API keys
Restrict the API keys so they are accepted only from the build platform's IP address ranges
explanations: Vaulting with rotation is a genuine improvement, but a static secret still exists at every moment and can be exfiltrated from any vault-integrated runtime - the root cause, standing long-lived credentials, survives the fix.

Federation lets the cloud provider trust the pipeline platform's own attested identity token and issue ephemeral credentials per job; no standing key exists to leak, commit to a repository, or steal, which removes the risk class instead of managing it.
Encryption protects stored copies, but the pipeline must decrypt the key to use it, so any compromised job still reads it in cleartext at runtime.
Source-IP restrictions are a compensating boundary that shared egress ranges and compromised build agents inside those ranges routinely defeat.

stem: Attackers tried the password 'Autumn2026!' exactly once against every account in a company's cloud email tenant and successfully logged in to nine mailboxes. Account lockout was configured at five failed attempts. Which control would MOST effectively have prevented these compromises?
options: Reducing the account lockout threshold from five failed attempts to three
Requiring all users to change their passwords every 45 days
Enforcing phishing-resistant multifactor authentication on all logins
Increasing the minimum password length from eight characters to twelve
explanations: Password spraying makes a single attempt per account, so no per-account counter ever approaches even a threshold of three; tightening lockout mostly enables denial-of-service against legitimate users.
Frequent forced changes are precisely what push users toward seasonal patterns like 'Autumn2026!'; scheduled rotation feeds this attack rather than stopping it.
With MFA enforced, a correctly guessed password alone cannot complete authentication, so all nine compromises would have been blocked regardless of how predictable the passwords were.
'Autumn2026!' is already eleven characters and satisfies typical complexity, so a modest length increase does not remove predictable patterned choices from the population.

stem: A strategy consulting firm serves two competing pharmaceutical clients. Compliance requires that once a consultant opens either client's deal documents, that consultant must automatically be barred from ever opening the competitor's documents. Which access control model is designed for this requirement?
options: Role-based access control with mutually exclusive client roles assigned at hiring
Mandatory access control using sensitivity labels and clearances
Discretionary access control with owner-managed ACLs on each client's folder
The Brewer-Nash model, which restricts access dynamically based on the subject's access history
explanations: Mutually exclusive roles enforce static separation of duties fixed at assignment time; here consultants may legitimately serve either client until their first access creates the conflict, a condition static role assignment cannot express.
MAC compares clearances against labels, but a consultant would be equally cleared for both competitors; the deciding factor is prior access history, which labels and clearances do not track.
DAC lets resource owners grant access at their discretion, which is exactly what must be overridden - no owner's decision can be allowed to breach the conflict-of-interest wall.

Brewer-Nash (the Chinese Wall model) was created for consultancy conflict-of-interest situations: datasets in a conflict class all start out available, and a subject's first access dynamically forecloses every competing dataset thereafter.

stem: A departing engineer's directory account was disabled on their last day, yet three weeks later VPN logs show new successful connections attributed to that engineer. The VPN concentrator authenticates users solely by client certificates issued from the corporate CA. What gap in the deprovisioning process MOST likely allowed this?
options: The leaver process never revoked the engineer's client certificate, which the VPN continued accepting independently of the directory
The VPN session timeout allowed an existing session to remain connected for three weeks after the disablement
The directory disablement had not yet replicated to the domain controller consulted by the VPN
The engineer's account was disabled rather than deleted, leaving the identity available for reuse
explanations: Certificates are self-contained credentials: a VPN that validates only certificate signatures and revocation status will accept a still-valid certificate regardless of directory state, so termination must include certificate revocation and the VPN must check CRL or OCSP.
Session persistence could explain one lingering connection, but the logs show fresh successful authentications occurring weeks later - a stale session is being confused with new logins.
Directory replication converges in minutes to hours, not weeks - and the stem states the VPN does not consult the directory for authentication at all.
A disabled account cannot authenticate anywhere the account is actually checked; the disable-versus-delete distinction is irrelevant when the authentication path bypasses the directory entirely.

stem: Forensic analysis confirms that attackers exfiltrated the database in which an authentication server stores the shared secret seeds for all employees' TOTP soft tokens. Passwords were not exposed. What must the organization do to restore the integrity of its multifactor authentication?
options: Force an immediate password reset for every employee account
Revoke all existing tokens and re-enroll every user with newly generated seeds
Shorten the TOTP code validity window from 60 seconds to 30 seconds
Temporarily block logins from unrecognized locations until the investigation concludes
explanations: Passwords were not part of the breach, and resetting them leaves the attacker able to compute every user's valid one-time codes from the stolen seeds - this remediates the wrong factor.

TOTP security rests entirely on the secrecy of each shared seed; once seeds are exposed, every future code is computable by the attacker indefinitely, so the only remedy is invalidating them all and enrolling fresh secrets into better-protected storage.
The attacker derives codes from the seed and current time exactly as the server does; the validity window governs clock tolerance and replay margin, not an adversary who holds the seeds themselves.
Location-based blocking is a temporary compensating filter that a proxy in a plausible region trivially evades; the stolen authentication factor remains fully valid.

stem: An architect discovers that RADIUS authentication traffic between branch-office network access servers and the central data center crosses a third-party WAN. The review notes that RADIUS obfuscates only the User-Password attribute, leaving usernames, accounting data, and other attributes readable in transit. Which remediation BEST protects this traffic?
options: Replace the shared secrets on all RADIUS clients with much longer random values
Migrate the branch network devices from RADIUS to TACACS+
Tunnel the RADIUS exchanges over TLS (RadSec) or an IPsec VPN between the sites
Enable RADIUS accounting so that any interception attempts generate log entries
explanations: The shared secret keys the password-hiding mechanism and authenticates messages, but even an excellent secret leaves every other attribute crossing the carrier network in cleartext - secret strength is not transport protection.

TACACS+ encrypts its payload but is oriented to device administration and is not a drop-in replacement for RADIUS-based network access authentication such as 802.1X; its legacy obfuscation is not modern cryptography either.

Wrapping RADIUS in TLS (RadSec) or IPsec provides mutually authenticated, fully encrypted transport for the entire exchange across the untrusted WAN, remedying the protocol's known cleartext exposure without redesigning authentication.
Accounting records session events at the servers; it can neither detect nor prevent passive interception occurring on a third-party carrier's infrastructure.

stem: A bank's corporate customers authenticate to the payment portal with passwords plus hardware OTP tokens, yet fraud continues: banking malware on customer PCs waits for a legitimate login and then silently submits wire transfers inside the authenticated session. Which control BEST addresses this fraud?
options: Require customers to enter a second OTP code at the start of every portal session
Deploy continuous behavioral biometrics to detect account takeover during active sessions
Reduce the portal's idle session timeout from thirty minutes to five minutes
Require out-of-band confirmation on a separate device that displays each transfer's payee and amount for approval
explanations: The malware acts only after all login-time challenges succeed; piling on session-start authentication cannot distinguish transactions the genuine user never initiated.

Behavioral biometrics detects a different actor driving the session, but here the legitimate customer is present and typing while the malware submits transfers in the background, so observed behavior looks entirely genuine.
Idle timeouts curtail abandoned sessions; this fraud occurs precisely during active, legitimate use of the portal.

Verifying each transaction on an independent channel shows the customer the actual payee and amount before execution, so malware-injected or altered transfers fail approval - authentication becomes bound to the transaction, not merely the session.

stem: Domain administrators already use separate privileged accounts, yet investigators find attackers captured those credentials with a keylogger delivered by a phishing email opened on an administrator's everyday workstation - the same machine used for domain administration. Which control BEST prevents recurrence?
options: Issue dedicated, hardened privileged access workstations used exclusively for administrative tasks
Require administrators to reach servers through a jump host from their everyday workstations
Shorten the rotation interval for all privileged account passwords
Deploy endpoint detection and response agents on the administrators' workstations
explanations: The breach happened because privileged credentials were typed on a machine exposed to email and browsing; a locked-down PAW that never touches those high-risk activities removes that exposure by design rather than by detection.

A jump host centralizes the access path, but the administrator still types privileged credentials on the compromised everyday workstation, where the keylogger captures them and malware can ride the session - the intermediary does not clean the endpoint.
Faster rotation shrinks each password's validity window, but the keylogger simply harvests every new password the moment it is used.
EDR is detective and depends on recognizing the malware; prevention in this scenario means never mixing privileged work with the risky general-purpose environment at all.

stem: During a penetration test, the team extracts crackable authentication material for several Active Directory accounts without ever authenticating, simply by requesting authentication-server replies for accounts flagged 'Do not require Kerberos pre-authentication.' Which remediation BEST addresses the root cause?
options: Reset the krbtgt account credential twice to invalidate any forged tickets in circulation
Convert the affected accounts to managed service accounts with automatically rotated passwords
Re-enable Kerberos pre-authentication on the flagged accounts and protect any unavoidable exceptions with long random passwords
Shorten ticket lifetimes and tighten clock synchronization tolerances across the domain
explanations: Resetting krbtgt twice is the response to a golden ticket compromise, where forged TGTs already exist; it does nothing about offline cracking of AS-REP responses for accounts lacking pre-authentication.

Managed service accounts remediate Kerberoasting of service tickets; the finding here is AS-REP roasting, caused by the pre-authentication exemption rather than weak service-account password handling.

Pre-authentication forces the requester to prove knowledge of the password before the KDC returns encrypted material, removing the unauthenticated attack path; long random passwords protect the rare accounts that must keep the exemption.
Ticket lifetime and clock-skew limits constrain replay of captured tickets; they do not prevent an attacker from anonymously requesting crackable AS-REP data in the first place.

stem: An assessor connects to the corporate directory server without presenting any credentials and downloads every employee's username, email address, and group memberships. The directory already enforces LDAPS for all connections. What should the security manager require FIRST?
options: Disable anonymous binds so every directory query requires an authenticated and authorized connection
Migrate clients from simple binds to StartTLS so credentials are protected in transit
Store directory password attributes with a salted, memory-hard hashing algorithm
Enable directory auditing to record which entries each connecting client reads
explanations: Encryption did not help because no credentials were required at all; anonymous binds are an authorization gap, and closing them forces enumeration attempts to present a valid, authorized identity first.
This confuses transport protection with access control; the directory already encrypts sessions with LDAPS, and the assessor never sent credentials that could be intercepted.
Hashing protects stored secrets if the database itself is stolen; it does not stop an anonymous connection from reading attributes the directory willingly serves.
Auditing is a detective measure that records the enumeration after the fact; the requirement is to prevent unauthenticated reads in the first place.

stem: A media company is building an app for smart televisions that have no keyboard and cannot present a browser login form. Users should authorize the TV app from their phones without ever typing credentials on the television. Which OAuth 2.0 flow BEST fits this requirement?
options: Authorization code flow with PKCE executed in a browser on the television itself
Device authorization grant, where the television displays a short code the user enters and approves on a second device
Resource owner password credentials grant, letting the television collect the username and password directly
Client credentials grant using an application identity provisioned to the television
explanations: PKCE protects the authorization code in apps that can drive a browser-based login; the scenario states the TV cannot present a browser form, which is the exact gap the device grant was designed to fill.

The device authorization grant exists for input-constrained devices: the TV polls the authorization server while the user completes login and consent on a phone or laptop, so no credentials ever touch the television.
The password grant makes the client application handle raw credentials and is deprecated; it recreates the very problem of typing passwords on the television.
Client credentials authenticate the application itself for machine-to-machine calls with no user context; the TV app must act on behalf of an individual user's account.

stem: A mobile banking app issues short-lived access tokens alongside long-lived refresh tokens. Threat modeling shows a refresh token stolen from a compromised device could silently maintain account access for months. Which control BEST limits this exposure while preserving the seamless login experience?
options: Shorten access token lifetime further so any stolen token expires within minutes
Require the password again whenever a new access token must be issued
Validate audience and issuer claims on every token presented to the API
Rotate the refresh token at each use and revoke the whole token family if a superseded token is ever replayed
explanations: This targets the access token, but the modeled threat is the long-lived refresh token, which the attacker can keep exchanging for fresh access tokens no matter how short their lifetime is.
Re-prompting for the password eliminates the refresh token's purpose and destroys the seamless experience the requirement preserves; it is constant re-authentication, not token risk management.
Audience and issuer validation stops tokens minted for one application from being replayed against another; it does not help when the stolen token is genuinely valid for this very API.

Rotation makes every refresh token single-use, and reuse detection reveals theft: when the legitimate client and the thief present the same superseded token, the server revokes the entire family, capping the stolen token's useful life without adding login friction.

stem: Attackers email employees a link to a convincingly named third-party application that requests OAuth permissions to 'read your files and mailbox.' Several users click Accept, and the attacker's application retains access even after those users change their passwords. Which response BEST prevents recurrence?
options: Require administrative review before third-party applications receive delegated permissions, allowing only vetted publishers and scopes
Enforce multifactor authentication for all users so their credentials cannot be captured by the phishing site
Shorten single sign-on session lifetimes so any attacker session expires within hours
Block the sending domains at the email gateway and schedule refresher phishing awareness training
explanations: Consent phishing abuses the authorization grant itself, so the preventive fix is governance of consent: administrator approval and publisher vetting stop users from delegating mailbox and file scopes to arbitrary applications.

This treats the incident as credential phishing, but no password was stolen; the users authenticated legitimately and then authorized the attacker's app, which keeps its tokens even after password changes and MFA enrollment.
This confuses interactive user sessions with durable OAuth grants; the malicious application holds its own tokens and can refresh them regardless of how quickly user sessions expire.
Blocking known domains and awareness training address one delivery vector, but attackers rotate infrastructure cheaply; without consent governance the next lure succeeds the same way.

stem: Employees authenticate with passwords plus app-generated one-time codes. A phishing campaign lures users to a reverse-proxy site that relays the credentials and codes to the real portal in real time, capturing the resulting sessions. Which change BEST prevents this attack from succeeding?
options: Issue hardware one-time-password fobs in place of the authenticator app codes
Lengthen the one-time codes and reduce their validity window to thirty seconds
Deploy phishing-resistant authenticators whose cryptographic response is bound to the legitimate site's origin
Block newly registered domains at the web proxy and train employees to verify URLs before logging in
explanations: Hardware fobs change where the code is generated, not its nature; any code a user can read and type can be relayed through the proxy just as quickly.
The proxy forwards codes within seconds, so freshness limits do not break the attack; real-time relay defeats any human-enterable one-time value.

Origin-bound authenticators such as FIDO2 credentials will not respond to the proxy's look-alike domain, so the relayed login fails cryptographically no matter how convincing the page is or how fast the relay operates.
Filtering and awareness reduce exposure but depend on catching every domain and every user decision; a determined campaign needs only one miss, so this cannot be relied on to prevent the compromise.

stem: A year after rolling out passkeys, a company still allows password-plus-SMS login 'for users who lose their devices.' Phishing reports show attackers now simply direct victims to the fallback login page. What is the BEST way to address this weakness?
options: Rate-limit the fallback login page and add bot detection to slow automated credential abuse
Convert the fallback into a monitored, identity-proofed account recovery process instead of an always-available alternate login
Add push-notification approval to the fallback flow so users can deny attempts they did not initiate
Mandate passkeys for administrators only and formally accept the residual risk for standard users
explanations: Throttling addresses automated guessing, but these are targeted phishing attacks using valid credentials and codes supplied by the victims themselves.

An always-open weaker path sets the real assurance level of every account; treating device loss as a supervised recovery event with verification comparable to enrollment closes the downgrade route while still supporting legitimate users.
Push approval remains a human decision the phishing flow can prompt for, and users under social-engineering pressure routinely approve; it does not remove the phishable path.

Scoping strong authentication to administrators leaves the general workforce exposed to exactly the campaign already underway; accepting a risk that has already materialized is not a defensible response.

stem: A manufacturer pilots fingerprint authentication on the shop floor. Several long-tenured machinists cannot register usable prints because of worn or scarred fingertips, though registered users authenticate reliably. Which metric should the evaluation team examine, and what does it imply for the rollout?
options: The false rejection rate, which measures how often legitimate enrolled users are denied
The crossover error rate, which identifies the tuning point where the error curves intersect
The false acceptance rate, which measures how often impostors are wrongly granted access
The failure-to-enroll rate, which shows the strategy must provide an alternative authenticator for workers the sensor cannot register
explanations: False rejection applies to users who enrolled successfully and are later denied; the machinists never completed enrollment, so this rate does not capture them.
The crossover error rate balances false accepts against false rejects for sensitivity tuning; it says nothing about people who cannot register a template at all.
False acceptance concerns impostors passing as someone else; the problem here is legitimate workers who cannot even join the system.

Workers who cannot produce a usable template are counted by the failure-to-enroll rate, a population the accept and reject error rates never see; a workable strategy pairs the biometric with a fallback method for those users.

stem: A defense contractor wants fingerprint verification for facility access, but the workers' council objects to any central database of biometric templates that could be breached or repurposed. Which design BEST addresses the objection while keeping biometric assurance?
options: Store each worker's template only on a smart card that performs the match locally, so no central repository of biometric data exists
Encrypt the central template database and tightly restrict administrative access to it
Switch to facial recognition, which can be captured passively and feels less intrusive
Protect stored templates with the salted hashing methods used for passwords
explanations: Match-on-card keeps the template in the holder's possession and performs the comparison on the chip, so there is no central biometric store to breach or repurpose, which answers the council's objection directly.
Encryption reduces breach impact, but the employer still holds a central biometric collection that could be decrypted, subpoenaed, or repurposed, which is the very concern raised.
Changing modality does not change the architecture; facial templates in a central database raise the same breach and secondary-use concerns, arguably more given passive capture.
Password-style hashing requires exact-match comparison, but biometric samples vary between presentations, so templates cannot be verified through a one-way hash the way passwords are.

stem: Physical security reviews show the same badge recording two consecutive entries to the data center with no intervening exit, suggesting employees are passing one badge back through the door for a colleague. Which control MOST directly addresses this behavior?
options: A mantrap vestibule that admits only one person for each authentication cycle
Anti-passback logic that refuses a badge re-entry until a matching exit has been recorded
Continuously monitored CCTV cameras covering the data center entrance and corridor
Longer retention of badge-reader logs to support future investigations
explanations: A mantrap stops a second person slipping through on one authentication, but here each person enters alone using the same badge in sequence, which a vestibule would happily permit.
Anti-passback ties each entry to a corresponding exit, so a badge handed back through the door is refused on its second consecutive entry attempt, defeating the sharing behavior directly.
Monitoring can spot the behavior when someone is watching, but it is a detective measure dependent on operator attention; it does not refuse the duplicate entry.
Log retention aids investigations after the fact; it neither detects nor prevents badge sharing at the moment it happens.

stem: A company migrates servers into a shared colocation facility where the provider controls building entry and dozens of other tenants access the same data hall. Which measure BEST protects the company's equipment from other tenants who are legitimately inside the room?
options: Contract terms requiring the provider to escort all visitors while they are inside the data hall
Provider-operated CCTV coverage of the aisles with footage available on request
A locked cage or cabinet around the company's racks, with keys or credentials held only by its own staff
Full-disk encryption on every server the company hosts at the facility
explanations: Escorts govern visitors, but the threat identified is other tenants whose staff have legitimate standing access to the same room; they are not escorted guests.
Camera coverage is detective and provider-controlled; it may help investigate tampering but does not stop another tenant from reaching the equipment.

In a shared hall, other tenants are authorized to be in the room, so protection must move to the asset boundary; a dedicated cage or locked cabinet restricts hands-on access to the company's own personnel.
Encryption protects data confidentiality if drives are taken, but it does not prevent physical tampering, cable pulls, or theft of the hardware itself.

stem: An electric utility's around-the-clock control room uses one always-logged-on operator console because the vendor software cannot switch users quickly and regulators prioritize immediate operator response. Security policy requires individual accountability for all system access. What is the BEST course of action?
options: Enforce unique operator logons at every shift change and require operators to absorb the switching delay
Approve a permanent exception for the control room and formally accept the reduced accountability
Launch an emergency project to replace the vendor platform with one that supports rapid user switching
Document a time-bound exception with compensating controls (badge-controlled entry, shift rosters, cameras) and require user switching in the next upgrade
explanations: Forcing the delay trades a safety and regulatory requirement for a policy checkbox; imposing operational risk on a critical process to satisfy the letter of a control is not sound risk management.
Acceptance without mitigation leaves no way to attribute control-room actions to individuals; exceptions should carry compensating controls and an expiry date, not a permanent waiver.
An emergency replacement of a certified operational platform introduces its own safety and availability risks and takes years; it is a long-term consideration, not the best present action.

When a control conflicts with safety and availability obligations, the risk-managed answer is a documented, time-bound exception with compensating controls that restore accountability by other means, plus a roadmap to close the gap permanently.

stem: A payroll database can be queried only between 07:00 and 19:00 on weekdays and only through the payroll application's front end; direct connections are refused even for valid accounts. Which access control approach do these restrictions illustrate?
options: Context-dependent access control, which evaluates when and how access is attempted before allowing it
Content-dependent access control, which filters what is returned based on the sensitivity of the records
Discretionary access control, because the payroll data owner chose to impose the restrictions
Mandatory access control, because individual users are unable to override the restrictions
